lead: A list is a mutable ordered sequence: one name can hold many items, and the items can be changed after creation. Unlike a string, a list can grow, shrink and have any position replaced. This matters for marks, prices, sensor readings and UPI transaction logs, where a program collects many values and edits them as work proceeds. The main danger is that two names may point at one list, so a change through one name appears through the other.
prereq: You need 3.1 for indexing and slicing, and Unit 1 for assignment, id() and operators.

blocks.text: A list literal is written in square brackets. Items are separated by commas and may have different types: [10, 'UPI', 3.5, True]. The empty list is []. A list is ordered, so each item has a position: index 0 is first, index -1 is last. Indexing and slicing work as for strings (see 3.1).
Lists can be nested. In marks = [[80, 75], [90, 88]], marks[1][0] is 90: first choose row 1, then column 0. A nested list is an item that is itself a list.

The operator + joins two lists into a new list; * repeats a list. Neither changes the original. in tests membership by equality. == compares length and then each pair of items; ordering (<, >) compares item by item, left to right, and stops at the first difference. A shorter prefix is smaller. For example, [1, 2] < [1, 3] is True and [1, 2] < [1, 2, 0] is True. Mixed types may raise TypeError because they cannot be ordered.

Methods are functions attached to a list. The changing methods below — append, extend, insert, remove, pop, clear, sort, reverse — edit the same list object and return None. The non-changing methods index(x), count(x) and copy() return a value and leave the list as it is.

items: append(x) adds one item x at the end. extend(items) adds each item from items. a.append([4, 5]) adds one nested list; a.extend([4, 5]) adds two items.
insert(i, x) puts x before position i. remove(x) deletes the first item equal to x and raises ValueError if absent. pop() removes and returns the last item; pop(i) removes and returns position i.
clear() removes all items. index(x) returns first position of x and raises ValueError if x is absent; it never returns -1. count(x) counts equal items.
sort() sorts in place; sort(reverse=True) sorts descending. reverse() reverses in place. copy() returns a shallow copy.

blocks.text: sorted(a) returns a new sorted list and leaves a unchanged. a.sort() changes a and returns None. del a[i] deletes by position; del a[i:j] deletes a slice. Use remove by value, pop by index when you need the removed item, and del by position when you do not.

Assignment does not copy a list. In b = a, the name b is bound to the same object as a. id(a) gives the object's identity (its address in CPython); a is b returns True when both names point to one object. == compares contents, so equal lists can have different identities. A change through a, such as a.append(40), is visible through b. Some syllabi say b holds a reference to the same object; no copy, not even a shallow one, is made by assignment.

a[:] and a.copy() make a new outer list. For a flat list of numbers or strings, the copy is independent: changing one list does not change the other. This is a shallow copy: it copies the outer list only, not the objects inside it. If an item is itself a list, both copies still point to that inner list (some syllabi call this a surface copy).
Example: n = [[1], [2]]; m = n.copy(); m[0].append(5). Then n[0] is [1, 5] because n and m share the inner list. Adding m.append([3]) changes only m's outer list.

figure.caption: Names a and b reach the same list object, so a change through a shows through b; c was made with a slice and owns its own list.

spec.aria: Two names a and b point to one list object while c points, with a dashed arrow, to a separate copy.

examples.question: For a = [10, 20, 30]; b = a; c = a[:]; a.append(40); a[1] = 99, give a, b, c and the values of id(a) == id(b) and id(a) == id(c).
steps: b = a: b is bound to the same object X.
c = a[:]: c is a new list with identity Y and contents [10, 20, 30].
a.append(40): object X becomes [10, 20, 30, 40]; b sees the same object.
a[1] = 99: object X becomes [10, 99, 30, 40]; b sees the same object.
id(a) == id(b) is True because both names point to X; id(a) == id(c) is False because c points to Y.
examples.answer: So a and b are [10, 99, 30, 40], c is [10, 20, 30], id(a) == id(b) is True, and id(a) == id(c) is False.
examples.check:
a = [10, 20, 30]
b = a
c = a[:]
a.append(40)
a[1] = 99
for x in a:
    print(x)
for x in b:
    print(x)
for x in c:
    print(x)
print(int(id(a) == id(b)))
print(int(id(a) == id(c)))

traps: b = a does not copy: it binds a second name to one list. Use a[:] or a.copy() for a new outer list.
sort() returns None; sorted(a) returns a new list. Writing b = a.sort() sets b to None.
append([4, 5]) adds one nested list; extend([4, 5]) adds two items.
a[:] and a.copy() are shallow. For nested lists, use copy.deepcopy(a) from the copy module if you need independent inner lists.

quiz.q: What is the difference between append and extend?
quiz.a: append adds one item at the end; extend adds each item from an iterable.

quiz.q: Which list method removes by value, and which removes by position and returns the item?
quiz.a: remove(x) removes by value; pop(i) removes by position and returns the item.

quiz.q: Why can a change made through b be seen through a after b = a?
quiz.a: b = a binds b to the same list object as a, so both names share one object and one set of items.

quiz.q: After a = [1, 2]; b = a; a.append(3); b[0] = 9, what is a?
quiz.a: a is [9, 2, 3]: append adds 3 to the shared object, and b[0] = 9 changes the first item of the same object.

quiz.q: For a = [3, 1, 2]; b = sorted(a); a.sort(reverse=True), give a and b.
quiz.a: a is [3, 2, 1] after in-place descending sort; b is [1, 2, 3] because sorted returned a new ascending list.

quiz.q: For n = [[1], [2]]; m = n.copy(); m[0].append(9); m.append([3]), give n and m.
quiz.a: n is [[1, 9], [2]] because the inner list is shared; m is [[1, 9], [2], [3]] because the outer copy gained one item.

quiz.q: For a = [1, 2, 3]; b = a[:], what do a is b and a == b give?
quiz.a: a is b is False because the slice made a new object; a == b is True because the contents are equal.

beyond: Not for the exam. In real systems, lists are the default batch container: reading a CSV column, collecting API rows, or queuing jobs. When numeric work grows, programmers move to NumPy arrays (Unit 6) because lists store references to objects, not packed numbers. CPython grows a list by over-allocating spare slots so append is usually amortised O(1); search for CPython list over-allocation and copy.deepcopy. For linked structures, see Unit 6.
